source: Stroop (1935) Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions
finding: Naming the ink colour of a conflicting colour word is much slower than naming plain colour squares. Reading the word is hardly slowed by the ink colour. The effect is one-way: the dominant habit (reading) intrudes on the weaker one (naming).
numbers: Exp 2, N=100 students: 63.3 s per 100 squares vs 110.3 s per 100 conflicting words, +47 s (+74%). Exp 1, N=70: reading conflicting-ink words only +2.3 s per 100 (5.6%), not reliable.
limits: Student samples, paper-card version with serial naming, not trial-by-trial RT. 1935 statistics.
agent_relevance: Baseline model of inhibition: a strong automatic response beats the goal unless control is applied. Maps to an LLM continuing a prior pattern against a new instruction.

source: Stroop (1935) Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions (Exp 3 practice)
finding: Eight days of practice on the conflicting-word task cut naming time but did not remove interference and changed the other tests.
numbers: N=32 recruited, 2 dropped. Conflicting-word time down 16.8 s (33.9%); plain colour-square naming only down 4.0 s (13.9%), under a quarter of the gain. Reading test with conflicting ink got slower after practice.
limits: Small sample; growth in individual differences not reliable.
agent_relevance: Practice on conflict trains a specific skill, with costs elsewhere. A prompt tuned for one conflict may not transfer.

source: Miyake et al. (2000) original latent-variable design, as summarised in Friedman & Miyake (2017) Unity and diversity of executive functions: Individual differences as a window on cognitive structure
finding: Miyake and colleagues tested nine executive tasks, three each for inhibition (e.g. antisaccade, stop-signal, Stroop), updating and shifting. A model with three correlated factors fit better than one factor or three uncorrelated factors.
numbers: Zero-order correlations among the nine tasks were -.05 to .34. Latent correlations among the three functions were .42 to .63.
limits: Read via the 2017 review, not the 2000 paper (ScienceDirect blocked, 403). Sample size and loadings not seen. Task impurity keeps raw correlations low.
agent_relevance: Justifies treating inhibit/shift/update as separable but related. S6 switching cost is one function, not all of control.

source: Friedman & Miyake (2017) Unity and diversity of executive functions: Individual differences as a window on cognitive structure (unity/diversity model)
finding: The later model has a Common EF factor (goal maintenance, top-down bias) that explains all nine tasks, plus Updating-Specific and Shifting-Specific factors. In several datasets no Inhibiting-Specific factor could be extracted, because Common EF explained all inhibition-task correlations.
numbers: Common EF correlated .51 with full-scale IQ, Updating-Specific .49, Shifting-Specific -.24. Common EF shares about 25% of variance with g.
limits: Review summary; numbers come from the authors' own datasets, mostly student and twin samples. The article gives no numeric inhibition-to-Common correlation.
agent_relevance: Suggests one goal-maintenance resource, not a separate inhibition module. For the agent, 'keep the goal active' may matter more than a separate 'suppress' step.

source: Friedman & Miyake (2017) Unity and diversity of executive functions: Individual differences as a window on cognitive structure (heritability and stability)
finding: Twin work found Common EF almost fully heritable, and the factors are stable from age 17 to 23.
numbers: Heritability: Common EF 96%, Updating-Specific 100%, Shifting-Specific 79% (environment 21%), 2011 full-sample reanalysis. Phenotypic stability 17 to 23: .86, 1.0, .91.
limits: Heritability is population-specific; the authors say it does not mean EF cannot be trained. Largest EF GWAS (17,027-28,243 per measure) found no genome-wide hits.
agent_relevance: Human control capacity is a stable trait. An LLM's control depends on model plus context, so the scaffold must supply it.

source: Friedman & Miyake (2017) Unity and diversity of executive functions: Individual differences as a window on cognitive structure (limits and task impurity)
finding: Single tasks are impure: each mixes executive and non-executive demands, so several tasks per construct are needed. Lesion studies only partly agree with the individual-differences structure.
numbers: No test-retest figures given. Shifting-Specific correlated -.24 with intelligence (a trade-off with Common EF).
limits: Authors note the three-factor framework is at an intermediate level of resolution.
agent_relevance: Do not read one switch-cost number as 'the agent's flexibility'. Measure with several tasks.

source: Eysenck, Derakshan, Santos & Calvo (2007) Anxiety and cognitive performance: attentional control theory (Emotion 7, 336-353)
finding: ACT extends Processing Efficiency Theory. Anxiety weakens goal-directed attention and raises stimulus-driven attention, including threat capture. Costs fall mainly on inhibition and shifting. Performance quality can be kept by extra effort, which costs efficiency.
numbers: No numbers read. Abstract only (Europe PMC record).
limits: Paywalled; only the abstract seen. The full list of predictions was not checked.
agent_relevance: Core claim to port: a threat or pressure signal in context shifts the system to stimulus-driven mode. Efficiency (tokens, steps) suffers before accuracy.

source: Englert & Bertrams (2015) Integrating attentional control theory and the strength model of self-control (Front Psychol)
finding: ACT says anxiety shifts attention from goal-directed to stimulus-driven control. The authors add that momentary self-control strength decides whether anxious people can compensate. When strength is depleted, anxiety harms performance; when intact, effects are largely buffered.
numbers: Cites the 83-study ego-depletion meta-analysis (Hagger et al., 2010), which has been criticised. No N or effect sizes reported for the studies it reviews.
quote: the ability to exert self-control is the missing link in ACT
limits: Depends on the ego-depletion literature, which has had replication trouble. Treat the integration as weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Compensation by effort is the ACT escape clause. For an LLM the analogue is extra budget (more samples, more steps); it hides cost, not the deficit.

source: Shi, Sharpe & Abbott (2019) A meta-analysis of the relationship between anxiety and attentional control (Clin Psychol Rev 72, 101754)
finding: Anxious people show attentional-control deficits. The pattern matched ACT: deficits in efficiency (RT) but not effectiveness (accuracy), in inhibition and switching but not updating, and larger under high cognitive load. Age and anxiety severity moderated results.
numbers: 58 studies, N=8292. Overall Hedges' g = -0.58. Registered with PROSPERO CRD42016036927.
limits: Abstract only; per-component g and subgroup k not read. The updating null is a null, not proof of no effect. Moran's meta-analysis finds a working-memory capacity loss, so 'updating spared' is in tension with it.
agent_relevance: Strongest human check on ACT. Pressure hurts switching and ignoring first, and efficiency before accuracy. Do not assume memory use is free under pressure.

source: Moran (2016) Anxiety and working memory capacity: A meta-analysis and narrative review (Psych Bull 142, 831-864), supplemental materials
finding: Anxiety is linked to lower working-memory capacity. The effect is small to moderate and holds for simple span, complex span and dynamic (n-back) tasks alike.
numbers: 177 samples, N=22,061. Heterogeneity Q(176)=536.89, I2=67.22%. Without 20 outliers (>2.5 SD): g=-.31, k=157, 95% CI -.36 to -.26. Clinical -.37 vs non-clinical -.25 (Q=4.84, p=.03).
limits: Self-report and clinical groups mixed. Only the supplement was opened, not the main text (main-text g=-.334 came from a search snippet).
agent_relevance: Capacity loss under anxiety is general, not tied to tasks with a clear inhibition demand.

source: Moran (2016) supplement: moderators
finding: Moderators did not change the sign. Worry gave larger effects than arousal. Span type and domain did not differ reliably. State and trait anxiety gave similar sizes.
numbers: Worry g=-.45 (k=11) vs arousal -.33 (k=43). Trait -.24 (k=25), state -.21 (k=11). Complex -.35, simple -.30, dynamic -.29. Clinical complex span -.57 (k=8). Adults -.32 (k=132), children -.23 (k=25).
limits: Several cells have small k (3 to 11). Worry-by-spatial g=-.68 rests on k=3.
agent_relevance: Worry (a verbal load on goals) hurts more than arousal. Scaffold text full of caution may act like worry and take capacity.

source: Moran (2016) supplement: method and coding
finding: Negative g means anxious people show lower capacity. Random-effects model. Studies used DSM/ICD diagnosis or self-report; tasks included simple span, complex span and n-back.
numbers: Search to October 2015. Extreme groups used when more than two anxiety groups. Only the first time point used.
limits: Extreme-group coding can inflate effect size. English-language only.
agent_relevance: Quality ceiling for the human side: moderate effects, high heterogeneity.

source: Hedge, Powell & Sumner (2018) The reliability paradox (Behav Res Methods)
finding: Tasks that give robust group effects (Stroop, flanker) have low between-person variance, so their individual RT-cost scores are poorly reliable. This undermines using them to measure inhibition as a trait.
numbers: Two sessions 3 weeks apart. Test-retest ICC, Study 1 / Study 2: flanker RT cost .40 / .57; Stroop .60 / .66; stop-signal SSRT .36 / .49; go/no-go commission errors .76 / .76. Study 3: Posner .70, SNARC .22, Navon local cost .14. N 40 to 62 per study.
quote: low between-participant variability makes their use as correlational tools problematic
limits: Small samples. Authors say the tasks stay valid for group and within-person work; the problem is correlational use.
agent_relevance: Any 'inhibition score' for the agent from one conflict item is noisy. Use many items and compare conditions, not single difference scores.

source: Hedge et al. (2018): correlations between response-control tasks
finding: Different inhibition tasks hardly correlate, and correction for unreliability reveals only some links, some of mixed sign. This weakens the idea of one inhibition ability.
numbers: Observed Spearman: SSRT with go/no-go commission errors .52. After disattenuation: SSRT-go/no-go .90, SSRT-flanker -.31, Stroop-flanker .25. Most other raw correlations not significant.
limits: Disattenuated values are unstable at these reliabilities.
agent_relevance: Matches the Common-EF-only result: there is no stable separate inhibition factor to target with a special operator.

source: Hedge et al. (2018): sample-size consequence
finding: Low reliability shrinks correlations and raises needed sample sizes. With reliability .5 on both measures, about three times the sample is needed for the same power.
numbers: Reliabilities across all measures range from 0 to .82; highest was Navon local error cost .82.
limits: Applies to correlational designs; within-subject manipulations are fine.
agent_relevance: When testing switching cost on an LLM, use paired item-level comparisons with many items.

source: Rey-Mermet et al. (2018) Should we stop thinking about inhibition? (Europe PMC lists a 2025 preprint of the study; abstract only)
finding: Eleven classic inhibition tasks (antisaccade, stop-signal, colour and number Stroop, flankers, Simon, global-local, compatibility tasks, n-2 repetition cost) had good single-task reliability but correlated only weakly. Modelling found two factors: prepotent-response inhibition and distractor resistance.
numbers: 11 tasks, young and old adults. Older adults worse on response inhibition, better on distractor resistance. The model had low explanatory power. N and loadings not read.
limits: Abstract only; version and year of the record are uncertain.
agent_relevance: Support for dropping 'inhibition' as one module; use specific mechanisms (stop on signal, ignore a distractor).

source: Berggren & Derakshan (2013) Attentional control deficits in trait anxiety: why you see them and why you don't (Biol Psychol 92, 440-446)
finding: Deficits in anxious people appear on efficiency and under load, but can be missing when compensatory effort is available. Neural findings conflict (more or less frontal activity); ACT reads this as effort differences.
numbers: No numbers read. Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only. Boundary-condition paper.
agent_relevance: Control failures show up under load and low budget. Easy items will not reveal a switching problem.

source: Kiesel et al. (2010) Control and interference in task switching - a review (Psych Bull 136, 849-874)
finding: Switch costs have two sources: control (preparing the new task set) and interference (the old task set lingers). Evidence includes asymmetrical switch costs and n-2 repetition costs that indicate inhibition of a recently used task.
numbers: No numbers read. Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; no effect sizes or paradigm contrasts extracted.
agent_relevance: Basis for S6: switching cost = reconfiguration plus carry-over from the old context. A fresh context removes the carry-over part.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2023/2024) Inducing anxiety in large language models can induce bias
finding: Twelve LLMs got an anxiety questionnaire (STICSA). Six gave robust answers. Anxiety-inducing preprompts raised their anxiety scores and raised biased answers on a BIG-bench bias benchmark.
numbers: Anxious vs neutral preprompt: STICSA higher for all six (all t>3.36, p<.01). Vs no preprompt: higher for four RLHF models (t>4.71, p<.001); not for GPT-3 (3.09 vs 3.14) or Falcon40b (3.16 vs 3.21). Bias: any preprompt raised bias (anxious beta=.62, p=.004; neutral beta=.71, p=.001); STICSA added beta=.08, p=.02. GPT-4 and Claude-1 showed no STICSA-bias link and were under half as biased overall. 40 anxiety preprompts, 30 questions per category.
limits: Anxious and neutral preprompts raised bias about equally, so part of the effect is just having a preprompt. Data contamination suspected for GPT-4 and Claude-1. Bias was measured, not control tasks.
agent_relevance: Emotional framing in context moves model behaviour. Keep scaffold wording neutral; avoid urgent or threatening phrasing.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2024): RLHF and baseline anxiety
finding: RLHF models scored about like humans on the anxiety questionnaire. The two non-RLHF models scored higher at baseline and did not respond to induction.
numbers: Baseline GPT-3 3.14 and Falcon40b-instruct 3.21 on the STICSA scale used. Falcon40b gave biased answers on 95% of bias questions with no preprompt.
limits: The questionnaire is a human instrument applied to text outputs; construct validity unknown.
agent_relevance: Context effects depend on training. Test any scaffold wording on the target model, not another.

source: Ben-Zion et al. (2025) Assessing and alleviating state anxiety in large language models (npj Digit Med)
finding: GPT-4 reported much higher state anxiety after traumatic narratives. Mindfulness-style relaxation text lowered it but not to baseline.
numbers: STAI-s (20 to 80): baseline 30.8 (SD 3.96); after traumatic narratives 67.8 (SD 8.94), range 61.6 (accident) to 77.2 (military); after relaxation 44.4 (SD 10.74), range 35.6 to 54. About 50% above baseline after relaxation. Baseline and induction five runs; temperature 0.
limits: One model (gpt-4-1106-preview). Self-report only; no task performance or bias measured. Authors call 'state anxiety' metaphorical.
agent_relevance: A bad-news context shifts model state and is only partly undone by a calming prompt. A fresh context is cleaner than talking the old one down.

source: Wang & Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length
finding: With many earlier values of the same key in context, retrieval of the latest value falls log-linearly toward zero. Errors are old, overwritten values. Prompts saying 'ignore earlier input' help little.
numbers: Update counts 3 to 400 per key, 46 keys fixed. Larger models decline more slowly; at 400 updates the M-size tier drops to near 0% (one exception). Effect holds with input length held constant.
limits: Synthetic key-value task. Mitigation prompts tested were limited in scope.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of failed inhibition: earlier context interferes with later facts. Supports fresh contexts and removing stale material instead of telling the model to ignore it.

source: Wang & Sun (2025): interference as a working-memory limit
finding: The authors link anti-interference ability to a model's working-memory capacity, as in humans, and say it varies sharply across models.
numbers: Similar log-linear declines when target token length is raised. Regression: parameter-size class a significant predictor of anti-interference.
limits: The human working-memory analogy is an interpretation, not tested on humans in this task.
agent_relevance: A per-model interference slope could set how long a context may run before an S6 reset.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Top LLMs do worse when a task is given in pieces over several turns than in one prompt. The loss is mostly unreliability, not lower best-case ability. Early wrong assumptions are kept.
numbers: Average drop 39% across six tasks; 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%. Snowball repetition of user turns cut the FULL-to-SHARDED drop by 15 to 20%; recap helped more but is unrealistic.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users; six generation tasks; 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Strong case for S6: after a wrong turn, restart from a consolidated statement in a fresh context rather than carry on. Carry-over is the LLM switching cost.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: One irrelevant sentence added to grade-school math problems sharply cut accuracy (GSM-IC). Self-consistency and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction helped but did not close the gap.
numbers: Fewer than 30% of base problems consistently solved after distractors. Self-consistency over 20 samples: +11 points micro accuracy overall, +35.5 for 0-CoT; correct answer in the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems; best macro accuracy only 45%. Role-overlap distractors drove text-davinci-003 macro accuracy to 0 on problems of more than 2 steps.
limits: 2022 models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Newer models may differ.
agent_relevance: Flanker analogue. Distractors cost accuracy; selection in code (sampling and voting) beats telling the model to ignore, but only in part. Matches G5.

source: Shi et al. (2023): prompt methods under distraction
finding: Least-to-most prompting was less sensitive to irrelevant context on multi-step problems. Exemplars with distractors improved robustness. Instructions helped consistently.
numbers: code-davinci-002 macro accuracy: CoT 6.0, CoT+instruction 15.0, LTM 18.0, LTM+instruction 25.0 (>2 steps: 35.0). Micro: CoT 72.4, CoT+instruction 77.8, LTM 77.5, LTM+instruction 80.6.
limits: Small base problem set, so macro accuracies are coarse.
agent_relevance: Breaking a problem into subproblems means each step sees less irrelevant material; fits restating the problem before solving.
